segments.he: פעם אחת נסע הזקן משפאלי להרב הצדיק מבארדיטשוב לדבר דברי שטות שלו כי כן הי' דרכו לנסוע להצדיקים להלשין ולדבר דברי לשון הרע של שטותו ושקר גביית עדות של שקר ונקבצו אז כמה וכמה צדיקים גדולים לבית הרב הצדיק מבארדיטשוב ז"ל כדי להחרים ולנדות את הזקן עבור שמבזה ת"ח אמיתי הוא רבינו ז"ל חינם על לא דבר כמובא בחיי מוהר"ן. אבל אשתו של הרה"צ מבארדיטשוב ז"ל בלבלה הדבר ונכנסה בתוכם יחף ונתבלבל הדבר וקילל אותה שהרגלים שלה יתנו בראנציק רח"ל ויראה מאד מהקללה ונתנו לה תלמיד הרה"צ מבארדיטשוב זצ"ל עצה שתלך בגרביים שחורות כדי שיתראה כמו בראנדיק וכן היה שתמיד הלכה בגרבים שחורות כידוע (מפני מה מסרה נפשה כ"כ בשביל הזקן כי הזקן החזיק אותה בפרנסתה וגם נתן לה הרבה כסף כל שנה בשביל לחלק לעניים ובזה שיחד אותה ואמר אז רבינו הקדוש שבשביל זה היה לו עונש להרה''צ מבראדיטשוב ז''ל ששנה שלימה התפלל בפשיטות בסידור כמו ילד ולא השיג השגות שהיה משיג מקודם שהיה רואה המלאכים שאומרים שירה ורבינו ז''ל אמר שהיו נוטלין ממנו כל מדרגותיו אך הוא חס מאד על טירחותיו ויגיעתו שכל מדרגתו באו לו ביגיעה ובטירחה גדולה ובאמת היה ידיד נאמן לרבינו ז''ל ופ''א הלך בדרך לביהמ''ד ורבינו ז''ל אמר אז בירכת השחר ושמע הרה''צ מבארדיטשוב ז''ל וניתפעל מאד ואמר ר' נחמענע'ס ברכות קלונגען און יאלע עולמות. וגם רבינו ז''ל בעצמו לא יניח שיכנסו להרב מבארדיטשוב התנגדותו עליו מפני שחס עליו כנ''ל ופ''א כשראה ברוח קדשו שהזקן נוסע אצלו נסע ג''כ אצלו וניתוועד יחד אצלו וכימעט שנעשה שלום אך הוא ירא מהעולם מה יאמרו העולם והגבירים שלו מדוע חלק עליו בחינם וכו' ופ''א כשראה רבינו ז''ל שהזקן נוסע והוא אצל הרב מבארדיטשוב ז''ל שלח את ר' נתן ור' נפתלי כמובא בימי התלאות.
segments.en: Rabbainu told a story that the Ba'al Shem Tov had told — about a certain poritz who had a Jewish innkeeper who had held his lease for a long time. Then a time came when he could not pay his rent, and the poritz placed the Jew and his household in a pit, and so forth. And this poritz had no children at all. And specifically after this terrible event, a son was born to the poritz. This is the matter of the justification of Divine judgment — "Your righteousness is like the mountains of G-d; Your judgments are a great deep" — meaning: even though Your judgments are a great deep [the just judgment of Hashem is not seen with the eye, and it appears that the judgment is buried and hidden to the depths of the great deep] — nonetheless we must know and believe that "Your righteousness is like the mountains of G-d" — that in this very matter Your righteousness is as the mountains of G-d — very great — and His mercy is very great, and everything is in justice and uprightness by what we do not understand greatly. Yet one must never, ever reflect negatively about Hashem, for "all His paths are faithfulness, and there is no iniquity — righteous and upright is He."

segments.he: ורבינו ז"ל הי' מחזיק את הרה"צ מברדיטשוב ז"ל לגדול המפורסמים שבדורו ואמר עליו שהוא שר על עולמות ועל הרה"ק ר' ברוך ז"ל אמר שהוא שר על רבוא רבבות ושהסתכלות על הפנטאפיל שלו מסוגל לתיקון הברית, ועל הרב שהוא שר אלף ועל הרבי מלובלין ז"ל שהוא שר מאה אבל הם ברוסיה: ופ"א הי' הרה"צ מברדיטשוב ז"ל אצל הרה"ק ר' ברוך ז"ל עם עוד צדיקים גדולים ושאל הרב מברדיטשוב השאלה שתמיד הרמב"ם עם הראב"ד חולקים שהראב"ד משיג השגות על הרמב"ם ובמה הם משתווים יחד ונשארו כולם משתוממים וענה הוא בעצמו (הרב מבארדיטשוב) בהתלהבות ורעש גדול עד שהפיל הכל מהשלחן. שבדבר זה הם משתנים יחד ,באחדות הבורא בזה הם משתווים יחד.
segments.en: And Rabbainu said that the matter of the Rosh HaShanah gathering at his grave is very great and very beloved in his eyes — and he said that even from the Heichal Ken Tzipor in Gan Eden [the palace of Mashiach — the highest of all the palaces] he would come to the gathering on Rosh HaShanah to pray together with them. [Just as we see that Hashem Himself leaves all the upper worlds and praises His Shechinah among those below — in the aspect of "and You are holy, enthroned upon the praises of Israel" — and "the Tzaddikim are found more in death than in life."] Rabbainu also said again how the Hidden Book is great and the Burnt Book is great — but to be with him on Rosh HaShanah is even greater. [For Rabbainu had already said that there is nothing greater than this: "There is nothing greater than this!" — as printed in Chayay Moharan, see there.]

Regarding the matter that our fellowship say there is a tradition from Rabbainu that Breslov Chassidim should not intermarry with one another: once they wanted to make a match between the families of Reb Noson and Reb Naftali. And they sent Reb Yudel to ask Rabbainu [this was after his passing, for Reb Yudel had the remarkable ability to perform pidyonos and wonders, and would see Rabbainu after his passing and speak with him as with a living person]. He went to the holy grave and when he came back, he told them that Rabbainu had said: "I still have two good friends among my disciples — and the Adversary wants to make division between them." "Ikh hob nokh tsvey gute fraynd — vil der Ba'al Davar makhن tsvishn zey a bred." And the match was not made. And there is similarly a saying that our fellowship should not conduct business together — for the Adversary places himself with all his strength to create division among our fellowship and prevent love between them, and in the matters of marriage and business such conflicts readily arise. Therefore one must guard oneself from this.

segments.he: שנתן עד כה להגיע יהי רצון שנזכה כל שאר הכתבים
segments.en: The holy Tzaddik the Magid of Terhovitsa was the companion of the holy Tzaddik Reb Nachum of Chernobyl. Their custom was to alternate: one year the Magid of Terhovitsa would travel to Reb Nachum for Shavuos, and the next year Reb Nachum would travel to the Magid of Terhovitsa for Shavuos. And their practice was to dance together the entire night of Shavuos [for it is the aspect of a wedding — "the day of his wedding" refers to the Torah as the groom — and as cited in the holy Zohar, one must rejoice with the Shechinah and Knesses Yisroel the entire night]. In Reb Nachum's final years when he was weak and could no longer travel to the Magid of Terhovitsa, he would send his son the holy Tzaddik Reb Mordechai of Chernobyl to the Magid of Terhovitsa — and they danced the entire night as described. And this is the custom until today in Uman: immediately after eating on the night of Shavuos everyone comes to the kloiz and dances together the entire night — literally without a single pause in the dancing, for these are saying a little of the Tikkun Shavuos while those dance, and so it alternates — and so forth.

Rabbainu said: on the night of Shavuos the primary awakening is to stay awake the entire night — and on Hoshana Rabba the primary thing is the saying. "Shavuos iz der ikar dos hofn zayn — un Hoshana Raba iz der ikar dos zogn."
Rabbainu said: "I would want to have my gathering in Eretz Yisroel." "Ikh volt gevolt hobn maynem a kibutz in Eretz Yisroel."

And Rabbainu said he envied Reb Yoskel — a very simple man who had a very large and thick siddur with all the old supplications and all the yotzros for every Shabbos of the year. His custom was to go to the house of study every day with his thick siddur and not to move from there until he had begun from the beginning: Modeh Ani — and recited everything in order — even all the Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur prayers, Pesach, Sukkos, all the blessings, the shofar blessings, Bircas HaMazon, wedding blessings, circumcision blessings, and so forth — all of it until the end — finishing the entire siddur from page to page every day. And Rabbainu envied him — for simplicity is highest of all.

[I heard a similar story about the Ba'al Shem Tov — who also envied such a simple man in his day, and said that every time he recited the prayers and psalms for Pesach, a Pesach rectification was made in the Heavens above, and so for Shavuos, and so forth. And also the well-known story of the Bread of the Presence in the time of the Ari: a simple man heard the sermon of the great Rav about the great rectifications that were achieved during the time of the Temple through the Bread of the Presence, and asked him what it was and how it was made. The Rav told him the full procedure of its making. He went home and agreed with his wife to make Bread of the Presence every week — to knead it through thirteen siftings and to bring it in the Holy Ark every Friday and beseech Hashem to eat it and that it should be pleasing and sweet to Him. And the shammes would find it and think it had been left for him, and eat it for Shabbos. When he came later and did not find it, he thought Hashem had eaten it, and was greatly joyful. And so it went on for a long time. Once the man came to the house of study with his bread and went straight to the Holy Ark — and did not see that the Rav was there — and spoke his usual requests to Hashem to eat the bread. The Rav overheard and rebuked him: "Fool! Does G-d eat?" He asked who then was eating it, and learned it was the shammes. He said: "Then I will do teshuvah." The Rav was repeating the sermon he was to give the next Shabbos. The Ari sent for him — that he should command his household, for at the hour when he was to give the sermon he would die, G-d preserve us, because he had shattered the delight of Hashem. For from that simple man Hashem had received as much delight as from the Bread of the Presence in the Temple.]

Reb Sendir of Terhovitsa — called by all "Reb Sendir the Great" — was one of the great members of our fellowship, and the extremity of his awe and his service of G-d is impossible to estimate in the mind. He founded the Terhovitsa fellowship — who were servants of Hashem of our fellowship so extraordinary that they went beyond the bounds of the human and it is impossible to estimate or describe at all the extremity of their self-stripping from physicality and their self-sacrifice in their service. They would go at the beginning of summer to the forests and fields, engaged day and night in hisbodedus. When they went out they would sing in the known melody: "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not yet saved." The nature of their service and their burning passion is impossible to estimate. Reb Sendir their leader had been previously a simple man — and once as a young man he threw a shoe at his mother who had rebuked him. But afterward when he drew close to Rabbainu's Chassidus and became greatly inflamed for the service of Hashem, he would be in the forests and mountains and fields day and night in hisbodedus and prayer without cease — eighteen hours — in melodies that broke the heart, such that whoever heard him, even the most wicked, became a complete ba'al teshuvah. When he would cry out at the holy grave in Uman, he could be heard from one end of the city to the other. Once the Rav of Tcheryn and other great members of our fellowship were traveling, and their route went through the forests of Terhovitsa. They heard a voice and followed the voice until they felt literally the stripping away of physicality from the sweetness of the voice. They saw it was Reb Sendir — still in the forests — and he was crying out: "I hate those who observe worthless vanities — but as for me, I trust in Hashem!" saying it to himself: "Zog, Sendir: 'Sanas hashomrim havlei shav — va'ani el Hashem vatakhti!'" And the Rav of Tcheryn said to the others with him: "It seems we must already be ashamed before him." "Es hot azoy ponim az mir meygn zikh shoyn shemen far im." And Reb Avraham would travel to Reb Sendir on Shabbos to see his service and receive from him.

Once on Erev Rosh HaShanah Reb Sendir encountered one of our fellowship who was a great miser. After they came out from the holy grave, Reb Sendir spoke with him about charity — speaking words of arousal with his characteristic burning passion — until the miser was so moved by the very power of his words that he took out his entire wallet with all his coins and gave it to Reb Sendir to distribute as charity. And the following year on Erev Rosh HaShanah, when they again came out from the holy grave, Reb Sendir wanted to approach him to speak with him — and the miser began to cry out loudly: "He is coming to rob me again!" "Er geyt mikh shoyn barebn!" For he knew that if Reb Sendir approached him and spoke with him, it would be impossible for him not to give him his entire wallet again — and therefore he gave himself this strategy: simply not to let him approach at all.

Once the opponents threw stones into the kloiz in Uman. Reb Naftali was alarmed and said: "Because of this they will take more conscripts and more!" "Az men varft shteyer vet men nemen nokh nekritim un nokh nekritim." Reb Nachman of Tulchin replied: "Reb Naftali — they will yet take your own grandchildren too!" [meaning mockingly that that is not the right concern]. Rather: because they threw two stones, two precious souls will come to us. "In reward for two stones, two souls will come." "In sakhar fun tsvey shteyner veln tsi unz kumen tsvey nefoshos." And so it was — at that time two very precious souls drew close and afterward became among the greatest of our fellowship. They were Reb Baruch Ephraim and Reb Mendeli the Litvak. The story of how it happened: they were among the great disciples of the holy Tzaddik Reb Mendili of Lubavitch, the Tzemach Tzedek, and Reb Baruch Ephraim had been a chozzer [one who reviewed and transmitted the Rebbe's teachings] there for more than twenty years. After the Tzemach Tzedek's passing they did not want to remain with his son, and went to seek some Rebbe. They found a book from Rabbainu's books and it appealed to them greatly. They saw that the author was from Breslov — and wanted to go there. They thought this was Breslau in Germany — and traveled there. When they arrived, they realized this was a different city in Russia — and walked on foot until they were brought to Uman. And there they became great servants of Hashem.

Reb Baruch Ephraim was of very deep intellect and composed a book on Likutay Moharan called Bibi HaNachal — which was a very great work but was lost, and only the smallest fragment of it was printed after Parparaos LeChochmah. And Reb Avraham said that he took much from Bibi HaNachal for his composition of Beur HaLikutim. When Reb Baruch Ephraim prayed it was with such burning passion — he would cover his entire face with the tallis — and prayed in a whisper with great depth until sweat literally poured from the tallis down to the ground. And the Rav of Tcheryn sent him to print the books — and he printed Likutay Moharan, Parparaos LeChochmah, Likutay Tefilos, Likutay Eitzos, and the other smaller books, all in the Lemberg printing. And the son of Reb Baruch Ephraim was also of very deep and sharp intellect, and lived in Eretz Yisroel — his mind was so deep in the service of G-d and Torah that he did not even recognize his own wife's face. Once his wife tested him: when he was in the street, she approached him and asked: "Are you Nachman son of Reb Baruch Ephraim? What is the wellbeing of your wife?" And he did not recognize her at all. Near Reb Baruch Ephraim's passing, the Rav of Tcheryn went to visit him and said afterward that he feared for him — lest he die — because he had taken death very much into his mind, and thought carries great power. And when he passed away, for some time afterward his body remained warm from the movement of his deeply engaged mind. And the Rav of Tcheryn's practice was always — when people came to him on behalf of someone ill — to insist above all that neither the patient nor his relatives take into their minds, G-d forbid, that he will die. On the contrary — take into thought that he is not ill at all and that he is well, and in many cases this is what actually happened.

The Rav of Tcheryn gave Reb Baruch Ephraim two thousand gold coins for printing Parparaos LeChochmah, the new Likutay Eitzos, and the other smaller books. [The large books — Likutay Moharan and Likutay Tefilos — had a different story: a wealthy man in Breslov named Beril Leib Nekhilis was suddenly aroused to do a lasting rectification for his soul, knowing that the ultimate purpose is that "man is not accompanied by gold or silver." And when he recognized our fellowship as genuinely G-d-fearing, he decided to ask them what to do for his soul for eternity. He encountered one of our outstanding fellowship and spoke with him — and was told with great arousal. From then on he began to support our fellowship with regular weekly sustenance, and also gave money to print Likutay Moharan and so forth.] Reb Baruch Ephraim traveled with the money and printed the books. He returned with four hundred gold coins remaining. And the Rav of Tcheryn said: "Men darf aleyn shraybn un aleyn drukn un aleyn bazayn un aleyn lernen" — meaning: the Adversary places himself on the matters of Rabbainu so intensely that one must do everything oneself — write and print Rabbainu's books, as is known. He traveled without a passport. And the printing itself in Lemberg was done without permission — and he had enormous toil and exertion and self-sacrifice until the printing was complete. Afterward they searched for him with the books — and confiscated the books, giving them to the government bookbinder to use the pages for government book covers. But Reb Baruch Ephraim, through great effort and many pleas to the bookbinder — who was a religious Jew — after he found favor in his eyes, succeeded in arranging a scheme so that the bookbinder returned the books to him and used plain paper for the government covers. And Reb Baruch Ephraim himself was imprisoned in iron chains and remained imprisoned for some time — and could have spent all his days in prison. But Hashem helped: a fire broke out and everyone fled — and he fled too — until Hashem helped him and he returned home with the books.

And Reb Mendeli the Litvak, companion of Reb Baruch Ephraim, lived in Uman and his service was with great burning passion. People said of him that every day was with him: half a day of Yom Kippur and half a day of Simchas Torah — for until midday he prayed with such burning passion and arousal beyond all estimation, and afterward he would say to himself: "Mendeli — der Rebe hot dikh geheysin freylikh zayn — 'mitzvah gedolah lihyos besimchah tomid'!" [Mendeli — the Rebbe told you to be joyful — "It is a great mitzvah always to be in joy!"] Once the opponents slandered him before the governor, and the governor himself came to the kloiz to see him. He heard how he prayed and pleaded before Hashem with mercy, entreaty, and supplication — in a sweet, melodious voice. The governor was so moved that he shed tears and said: "If I were king I would give him whatever he wants." He was extremely poor — his entire livelihood was that at night he would make a few small cookies, and in the late afternoon after his prayer he would go to the marketplace to sell them. People would snatch them immediately, and other cookie bakers came close to him. And they said to him: "Reb Mendeli — what do you put into your cookies that people snatch them so?" He answered: "What can I tell you — they are kneaded in the weeping of midnight, and baked while in joy and song." For he kneaded them while reciting Tikkun Chatzos with tears — and baked them afterward in joy and song.

In the town of Teplik it was customary to hold a fair on Erev Rosh HaShanah — and therefore some members of our fellowship from there attended the fair and then traveled to Uman for Rosh HaShanah, arriving at midday [on Erev Rosh HaShanah]. Moharan'as was very displeased and said: "Rather than falling suddenly into Rosh HaShanah like this — it would be better not to come." "Eyder azoy araynfaln in Rosh HaShanah — iz shoyn gleykher nit tsi kumen." For Rosh HaShanah requires preparation — the memory of the covenant, from which comes the arousal to teshuvah — and Erev Rosh HaShanah at the holy grave with teshuvah, confession, heart-outpouring, and very great arousal [almost more than Rosh HaShanah itself].

Reb Avraham said: "It is true that Rabbainu said Hashem conducts the world more beautifully each time — but this is in the generality of the world. In the particular, each individual must fear that he will receive a slap on the face." "Ken zayn a sheyne velt on mir, khalile." [There can be a beautiful world without me — G-d forbid.] "And in any event one must not complain, G-d forbid — only bow one's head and accept with submission everything that passes, for the hero desires only submission — as it is written in the story of the Ba'al Tefillah, see there."

Once there was a person of our fellowship who was at Moharan'as's home on Erev Shabbos. He heard and understood from the dispute between Moharan'as's wife and him that he had nothing at all for Shabbos. And this person had at his home five rubles that he needed for his own Shabbos. He went and brought the five rubles and gave them to Moharan'as that he should use them for the holy Shabbos. Meanwhile, past the window came a mentally deficient man walking barefoot — and his feet were full of wounds and blood, for it was the season of Tevet with snow and frost. Moharan'as called him into the house and asked him: "Why are you going barefoot — why don't you buy yourself shoes?" He answered: "Because I have no money." Moharan'as asked him if with five rubles he could buy shoes. He answered yes. Moharan'as took the five rubles and gave them to him to go buy shoes for his feet.

The man who had given the five rubles to Moharan'as stood there full of questions and amazement: "I needed these five rubles for my own Shabbos — and only because I had mercy for your honor I brought them to you for your Shabbos. And in the end you found a mentally deficient man whom no one wanted to look at — and gave him the five rubles!" But he did not have the boldness to ask Moharan'as about this. Moharan'as, however, perceived that it was hard for him. He said to him: "Did you hear? Our Sages said: it is a great thing to pursue a commandment that has no one to perform it. And where is there a commandment more without someone to perform it than this? If I do not give him money for shoes — who will give him? [He could fall ill and die, G-d forbid.] And therefore, since it is such a commandment without someone to perform it — it supersedes my Shabbos and yours — just as our Sages ruled in the Megillah tractate that a meis mitzvah [a neglected corpse] supersedes every commandment in the Torah — even the reading of the Megillah — because it is a commandment with no one to perform it."

One great elder of our fellowship was humiliated and remained silent before his disgrace. They said to him: "Why are you silent? Honor of Torah is at stake!" He answered: "Believe me — with one word I could have silenced him. But the very reason I stayed silent and did not answer was for the honor of Torah — for it begins with the honor of Torah and ends with self-honor." "Es heybt zikh on mit kevod haTorah un lozt zikh oys mit kevod atzmo." [The apparent defense of Torah's honor is often only self-honor in disguise — therefore he preferred to remain silent entirely.]

Reb Yisroel of Kardan, who drew close to Rabbainu's Chassidus, had studied and served Reb Moshe of Breslov. Reb Moshe studied with him from Rabbainu's books — about the true Tzaddik who can perform twenty-four kinds of pidyonos [redemptions] and other matters, the spiritual levels of the true Tzaddik. Reb Yisroel replied that his own famous Rebbe also attained these levels [for he had previously been a very strong believer in the famous men of our time]. Reb Moshe replied: "You are a liar and your famous Rebbe is a liar!" "Du bist a sheker un dayn Rebbe iz a sheker!" And he refused to speak with him further. Some time passed and Reb Yisroel worked in the service of Hashem and came to understand the truth — and then he appeased Reb Moshe and studied with him afterward, and through him drew close to Rabbainu's Chassidus.

Reb Moshe of Breslov, a disciple of Moharan'as, was praying Minchah on Erev Rosh HaShanah in the kloiz. Once when he began to say the Ketoret: "And Hashem spoke to Moshe, saying..." he fell faint and had to be revived for a long time. They asked him why he had fallen faint. He answered: he had begun "And Hashem spoke to Moshe" and had contemplated: Hashem spoke with Moshe — a person of flesh and blood! A person of flesh and blood can purify himself so much that Hashem speaks with him! And he was so aroused from this that he fell faint. "Ikh hob zikh bay gerekhnt az der Aybershter hot geredt mit Moshe — der Aybershter hot geredt mit an adam — mit a basar vedam!"

Sir Moshe Montefiore wanted to build Reb Shmuel the Alef an upper room on top of a great house — but Reb Shmuel the Alef did not agree to this. Reb Shmuel would do heavenly consultations [ask questions and receive answers from Heaven]. These are the ones I remember: he once asked: "What should I study to attain fear of Heaven?" The answer: let him rise at midnight. He asked: "What shall I do — for my heart is like stone?" The answer: "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone." He asked: "Which section of the Tur should he study regularly?" The answer: "The second row — emerald, sapphire, and diamond" [meaning: Yoreh De'ah, which is the second section of the Tur]. He asked if he should travel to Uman to heal his hand [which had broken in the earthquake]. The answer: "I will bring them and plant them on the mountain of My inheritance" [meaning: do not travel far]. He asked if he should study Chabad. The answer: "Only from the Rav's books." He asked if he should study Kabbalah. The answer: "Should a woman ask her husband whether she may immerse and become pure?" [meaning: of course — there is no question.] He asked if it was fitting for his son to become wise [for he had a simple son]. The answer: "I said: I will become wise — but it is far from me." [Meaning: he will not grow wiser.] He asked about a certain ill person — would he live? The answer: "And he went toward the mourning." [He passed away.] He asked about another ill person. The answer: "In his merit" — i.e., in the merit of Reb Shmuel who is a mohel [he would be healed through his merit]. Once he drank beer at night with a light-minded person, and was told: "At night — and truth will not be in your mouth." And in the morning his wife brought him a cloth with a stain — and it made her impure. And from his grandson Reb Avner — a man whose mother told him: Reb Avner would sit the entire week in the Ari shul of the Sephardim in Tzfas, which is near the cemetery. This was his custom: immediately after a wedding [his own wedding] on motzei Shabbos he would go to the Ari shul and sit there serving G-d in Torah and prayer until Friday night — in complete solitude. And this was his custom for thirty years. He and his sister — still girls at the time — would bring food and drink to him there. Once in the middle of the week he came home, wounded and covered in blood — and it became known to no one, and he would not tell what had happened. And from then on he never went back to study there. His son told me as a great secret not to tell anyone. For the matter was: he was standing by the platform on high and studying. Suddenly he saw the Ari standing by him and speaking with him — and from the greatness of the fear and awe, he leaped from the platform [which was high] to the ground in a single leap and was wounded and covered in blood, and returned home. And from then on he never went back to study there.

Reb Naftali had a relative who studied philosophical investigations and so forth. Reb Naftali heard of this and said: "Master of the Universe — take him!" "Nem im tsi!" And so it was — he passed away immediately. When Moharan'as heard of this, he was angry about it and said: "This is not what we received from Rabbainu! Who knows what good children he could have had — and so forth."

Rabbainu once saw young men who studied a great deal. He said to them: "If you were close to me you would study less — but more." "Ven ir zent tsi mir mekurev volt ir vintsikoyer gelernt ober shoyn mer gelernt." [For they would be studying lishmah — for its own sake — with holiness, purity, and awe, turning Torah teachings into prayers.] And similarly with the holy Tzaddik of Berdichev: his father-in-law said to him that since becoming a Chassid he studies less than before. He answered: "Before, I had to study a little for my father-in-law, a little for my mother-in-law, a little for my wife, and a little at least for Hashem too — so I had to study a great deal to have enough for all of them. But now that I study only for Hashem — however much I study is enough."

The Rav Reb Shneur Zalman heard from the Great Magid, of blessed memory, that one who studies not for Heaven's sake forgets a certain Abaye and Rava passage in the Talmud — and the Magid named which one it was. Afterward it happened that the Rav came to a town of opponents, and a great scholar among them said he would show the Chassid that he cannot truly learn. He asked him: "How many Abaye and Rava debates are there throughout the entire Talmud?" The Rav answered: "You know." The scholar answered yes — and began to recite from his mouth: "Here there is an Abaye and Rava, and here" — and listed every Abaye and Rava debate in the entire Talmud. All except that one Abaye and Rava that the Magid had told him — the one that one who studies not for Heaven's sake forgets. That one he did not mention. And the Rav asked: "Is there no more?" He answered: "No." The Rav said: "But there is that Abaye and Rava!" — and named it. And the scholar's face turned like the bottom of a blackened pot. The Rav said: "Tell the people present — do not think I know this better than he — i.e., all those Abaye and Rava debates. I only know this one — from what I received from the Magid: that one who studies not for Heaven's sake forgets this Abaye and Rava. Therefore when he listed all the Abaye and Rava debates and did not mention this one — I remembered the words of the Magid."

In the days of Moharan'as, when conscriptions began, men would make themselves physically defective in order not to be taken for military service — some making themselves deaf and so forth, and some even blinding one of their eyes. When Moharan'as learned of this he was very displeased and said: "It would be more fitting to blind both eyes with weeping before Hashem — and through that, and through being awake at nights in Torah and prayer before Hashem, one would certainly accomplish far more."

At that same time of the military conscriptions, a woman had a son who was to be taken as a soldier. She went to the cemetery and wept so much that her soul departed from her. They told this before Moharan'as. He said: "What did she accomplish with this? She died — and she did not save her son. But if she had gone every day for an hour or more and prayed and pleaded before Hashem — she would not have died, and she would also have saved her son through this. And she would also have saved many, many Jewish souls through this."

Reb Shimshon of Uman, grandson of Rabbainu, once came to Berdichev. There was then one of our fellowship there — Reb Shimshon of Berdichev, a teacher [and he was the one who brought close Reb Shmuel Heshel who did [acts of holiness] in Siberia, and he passed away in Jerusalem and his resting place is on the Mount of Olives]. They were engaged together in the service of G-d. Suddenly in the middle of their conversation Reb Shimshon of Berdichev glanced at his watch — as if to say he had no time — and asked why he had no time now, since it was not the time for study in the cheyder. He answered that he had to go to the time set aside for groaning together with his wife: "Es miz di tsayt vos er darf zikh gayn aoys krektsn." And Reb Shimshon of Uman asked what he meant. He explained: when he is poor and destitute and his wife comes home and begins to complain and sigh — he has no other counsel but to help her sigh: "ir tsi helpn krektsn." For if he showed her a cheerful face, she would honor him well — but through the sighing he calms her and sets her at ease. Therefore he has a fixed time every day to go and help her sigh — so he has no time now.

And there was one of our fellowship who, when he was at home and wanted to do hisbodedus and groan during his hisbodedus [lying on his bed as described in Sichos HaRan] — he was ashamed and afraid that his wife would be angry at him. Therefore he tied his teeth together so she would think his teeth were aching — and then he would be permitted to groan.

The Rav of Tcheryn said: even though Rosh HaShanah in Uman is the greatest of all — and he believes this with complete faith — in terms of actual feeling, of sensing Hashem and arousal, he felt more at the last count of the Omer in Breslov [meaning the forty-ninth day of the Omer, before Shavuos eve — for they would come for Shavuos to Moharan'as in Breslov, arriving some days before, and the last count they would all count together with great arousal, such that the entire city could hear the counting. Therefore in terms of actual feeling of Hashem and arousal, he felt more at that counting than at anything else — even more than Rosh HaShanah in Uman. But in faith he believes that Rosh HaShanah is highest of all].

Once on Purim, Rabbainu's daughter Marat Chaya came to Breslov with her son Nachman and lodged at the home of one of our outstanding fellowship, Reb Mordechai. They told Moharan'as: "Rabbainu's daughter and her son Nachman are lodging on Purim at Mordechai's." And Moharan'as was greatly moved by the allusion [for he was always watching the allusions in every day's events] and said: "Did you hear what they told us — that Nachman is lodging on Purim at Mordechai's?" "Az Nachman shtayt on Purim ba Mordechai!" And so it was with other times too — such as Lag Ba'omer: at Reb Shimon's, and so forth.

In Tzfas in the time of Reb Shmuel the Alef there were Jewish ruffians — whoever they had a grievance against, they would kill him. They had swiftest horses that could fly almost through the air, and they would be in Beirut or Damascus during the day. They had their eye on Reb Shmuel the Alef to harm him — and they said they wanted to speak with him face to face, alone, with no one between them. The entire city feared that they would kill him. He said he was not afraid of them — only of Hashem. He met with them alone and spoke with them. A fear and awe fell upon them — and they did not touch him — and it was a wonder to the entire city.

Reb Shmuel the Alef grew up from his youth with the Seer of Lublin. His father Reb Avraham Peretz was among the disciples of the Seer of Lublin and was the Seer's ba'al toke'ah. And the Seer loved Reb Shmuel greatly and commanded his father to travel with him to Eretz Yisroel — and there he would perform wonders. And so from his youth his father traveled with him to Tzfas, where he afterward became the Chief Rabbi and Mara d'Asra. He was wise in all branches of wisdom — including the wisdom of medicine, in which he was greatly renowned. He was practically the physician for all those regions — and gentiles too would come to him by the hundreds and thousands from all their places to be healed. Many times he would travel to their villages or towns and stay with them several days and nights for their healing. And whatever they wanted to pay him as a fee he refused to accept — only telling them to instruct their children after them to be lovers of Israel, and that if they should see a Jew straying to bring him home. And so he always planted love of Israel in their hearts — and so it was until those days that they loved Israel more than in other towns of Eretz Yisroel — and in particular the grandchildren of Reb Shmuel they honored greatly, calling them "children of the Sage Shmuel" and saying they recognized them by their faces. And they told me that even on Rosh HaShanah he was in the house of study — and rows of Arabs and Arab women would stand outside in the streets, having come to be healed. He would go out before the shofar blowing — and at that time his mind was not at all free, as is well known for him before the shofar blowing. Nonetheless he would tell each one whatever came to his mouth for their healing — and so it was done until he had finished with them all. And after Yom Tov they all came with gifts and thanks. And all of this he did for love of Israel.

And he edited and helped print Reb Yisroel of Shklov's book Pe'as HaShulchan — and they made a great feast, at which Reb Yisroel was fasting a series of three days. He did not want to break his fast — and also did not want it known that he was fasting. Therefore he was compelled to eat at the feast, where everyone saw him — and in truth ate nothing from the feast, only managing cleverly so that everyone thought he was eating while in reality he was not at all. Reb Shmuel the Alef had the custom to bless all his grandchildren on Erev Yom Kippur. His sons would bring all his grandchildren to him. All of them he blessed — only one granddaughter he did not bless. They brought her to him again and he turned his face away and would not bless her. They brought her once more — and again he would not bless her. A few days afterward that granddaughter passed away, G-d preserve us. And they understood after the fact that he had known beforehand that a death sentence had been decreed upon her — and therefore he had not blessed her.

A certain woman — a truly righteous woman — told me that she was the eldest granddaughter of Reb Shmuel the Alef. Once she did him a great favor: his grandson, her uncle named Reb Avner, had Reb Shmuel prophesy over him even when he saw his daughter pregnant with him — he said to her: "You have conceived from a great soul — the soul of Avner son of Ner." And he was very precious in Reb Shmuel's eyes. Once when the boy was small he became upset and nothing could appease him — and this caused Reb Shmuel distress. She went and appeased him until he was calmed. When Reb Shmuel saw this he said to her: "For the good you have done me in this — I bless you that you will never suffer from stomach ailments, and whatever foods you eat will not harm you." And so it has been to this day — no food harms her and she has never suffered from stomach ailments.

Reb Avner told: when he was in Glupin, he made a siyum on the entire Talmud and made a feast with musical instruments. And he told his father that Reb Shmuel lived in the lower room and his son Reb Avraham — who was a great and wondrous person — lived in the upper room, closed and sealed there in the service of Hashem. And it was written in a handwritten manuscript of the Alshich that whoever studied the entire Alshich such and such times, the Alshich would come and study with him. Reb Avraham fulfilled this — studying the Alshich many times — and when he finished in the upper room he said: "Let our master fulfill what he promised." Suddenly the Alshich stood before him in a bright and beautiful form, radiant as the sun — beyond what he could endure — and Reb Avraham's face changed color and he could not speak. He immediately descended to his father Reb Shmuel and fell faint. They revived him and he told Reb Shmuel what had happened. Reb Shmuel said to him: "What is the novelty in this for you, and why were you so frightened?" [For Reb Shmuel was accustomed to such things.] Reb Shmuel was blind — and would play the violin and would not sleep sixty breaths [a very short sleep] at any one time. And they told me: I was a small child in his time and I would smell a fragrance literally like perfume from him [because my mother used to eat esrogim when she was pregnant with me]. And they would bring me to him in his lap and he would hold me in his lap and smell from me — and this gave him great pleasure. And every day they were required to bring me to him so he could smell from me.

My father told me that my grandfather Reb Yitzchak — my mother's father — son-in-law of Reb Shmuel, was a very sharp and great Gaon, well-versed in the entire Rambam with great sharpness and erudition. Before his passing, my father sat by his bedside — and suddenly he awakened and commanded that the Rambam be brought. He looked at it and said: "Good, good!" My father asked what this was. He answered: "Just now the Rambam came to me in a waking state and told me: because throughout all your days you studied greatly in my book Mishneh Torah — I have now come at the time of your passing to resolve for you all the difficulties you have in the Rambam." And he asked him what was difficult for him, and resolved it. Therefore he commanded that the Rambam be brought — to see if it was indeed resolved — and he saw that it was well resolved.

Elders of our fellowship who knew my grandfather Reb Shmuel the Alef — who was close to Rabbainu's Chassidus and kept Rabbainu's sister Perel in his home. The story that happened [which I also heard from my family]: once he did not know the explanation of a passage in the writings of the Ari — and he asked that the Ari come and tell him the explanation. And so it was — the Ari came to him and told him the explanation. But he sensed that the Ari was displeased at having been troubled. And so he went every Friday to the Ari's grave and said all of Tehillim to appease him — and this was a great burden for him, for he was the Mara d'Asra [city rabbi] and had no time. Yet despite this he fulfilled it. When Moharan'as came to Eretz Yisroel and was at Reb Shmuel the Alef's home, he explained to him the greatness of the ten chapters of Tehillim [the Tikun HaKlali] — and from then on, when he went to the Ari's grave, he recited those ten chapters. For he said: these ten chapters encompass all of Tehillim in their entirety. And Reb Shmuel the Alef had all of Rabbainu's holy books and would study in them.

Reb Shmuel the Alef was raised from his youth with the holy Seer of Lublin and became the Chief Rabbi and Mara d'Asra of Tzfas. He was a scholar in all areas of knowledge including medicine — and was practically the general physician for all the Galilee regions, with both Jews and Arabs — from all corners — coming to him by the hundreds and thousands to be healed. He never wanted to accept payment — only requesting that they love Israel and protect Jewish wayfarers. And indeed, they loved Israel there more than in other towns of Eretz Yisroel.

Reb Shmuel the Alef was present at the great earthquake of 5598 [1838] in Tzfas — when everyone died and he survived, though his hand was broken from the collapse of the building upon him. Yet despite this he continued writing. And the holy Tzaddik of Avritch [author of Bas Ayin] was a close disciple-companion of Reb Shmuel. He was at his house of study in Tzfas and said that whoever passed through his entrance would be saved — and so it appeared that those who stood under the arch where they stood remained alive while the wall remained standing. And once there was a plague, G-d preserve us, in Tzfas. The Rav of Avritch said that he would go as an atonement for Israel — that he would take the plague upon himself and remove it. He sent messengers to Reb Shmuel that he should come to him before his death as he had secrets to transmit. But Reb Shmuel refused to go — citing the Gemara: "When there is pestilence in the city — do not go out into the street." And so it was — the Rav of Avritch passed away and the plague ceased. And our aunt Sorah — the eldest daughter of Reb Shmuel — who was a small girl at the time, told us: once in the night when she was sleeping with her father, she woke and saw a harmful spirit stretching from the ceiling to the floor. She was greatly frightened. Reb Shmuel arose from his bed, looked in some book, and each time saw it diminish until it disappeared entirely. And Reb Shmuel never traveled even one amah outside the Holy Land. Once the Pasha of Acre was dangerously ill — and they sent for Reb Shmuel. He came up to the outskirts of the city — until the point where he knew that was the border of Eretz Yisroel — and would not go further. They were compelled to bring the Pasha on a stretcher to Reb Shmuel outside the city.

Reb Shmuel the Alef had a dispute with the Rizhiner — for the Rizhiner wanted to take control over all the charitable funds from Eretz Yisroel, and Reb Shmuel would not agree to this. The Chassidim of the Rizhiner asked him why he did not punish Reb Shmuel. He replied: "Because of the power of his Torah and the power of Eretz Yisroel I cannot do anything to him." And once they told Reb Shmuel that the Rizhiner says: "Land iz do un Yisroel bin ikh." [Land is here and Israel am I.] Reb Shmuel said this was heresy.

And our family told: once there was a drought in Tzfas and great scarcity — and no flour could be found to buy. Suddenly Arabs came to Reb Shmuel with many sacks of flour to sell — and he bought it for distribution to the city. When they came to pay the Arabs, they were not to be found — and until this day it is not known who those men were.

And once some Jews were traveling to Meron to the grave of Rashbi — and an Arab pursuer who was one of the great nobles pursued them and threw them into water until halfway on the road — and they could not be rid of him. What did they do? They took him and beat him so severely that he nearly died — and he became dangerously ill and was despaired of. He was the only son of his father, and his family and community prepared to take vengeance on Israel, having all the people of Tzfas in great danger. Everyone feared, and Reb Shmuel would sit by the Arab boy's bedside literally through the nights — not moving from the bedside. He prayed greatly there and increased his prayer. All those surrounding him said there was no natural way he could be healed — and Reb Shmuel announced the situation to the city. They went to the holy places and he increased his prayer by the bedside — until Hashem helped and the boy was healed in a miraculous manner. And the inhabitants made a holiday.

And the holy Rav of Avritch commanded Reb Shmuel to be a mohel [circumcisor] — and so he became the general mohel for all the surrounding area. Once he performed a circumcision and created an open urethra — and the boy urinated in drops. Reb Shmuel had a grievance with the Rav of Avritch — for he had commanded him to be a mohel. The Rav answered: "Do not fear — he will have a complete healing before his wedding." Many years passed and they saw the boy still urinating in drops. At the time of his wedding they came to the Rav of Avritch and asked if they should hold the wedding. He said yes. And on the day of the wedding ceremony the boy was completely healed — and was like any person and had children and so forth.

Concerning Reb Moshe Klain — one of our fellowship born in Eretz Yisroel who drew close to Rabbainu through disciples of Moharan'as: Reb Meir of Teplik and Reb Nachman of Avrohovsky, whose father lived in their neighborhood. His mother was pregnant with him and gave birth — and they thought he was a stillborn and suffered greatly and did not want to make the circumcision. But the disciples of Moharan'as took the child into their home, performed the circumcision, and promised that he would live a good life. And when the boy grew up he drew close to them and became their disciple. But his father — incited by the opponents — began to persecute him intensely, even to actual physical danger, and sat shiva over him, G-d preserve us, and expelled him from being a son. [They said to him about this: "Because of this I will not sit shiva over any more of my children" — and so it was, that over all his other children who died in his lifetime he sat shiva, but over him he had an unusually long life. And in his old age he was with him in honor and studied Rabbainu's book — and later regretted his opposition, saying he had not known the holiness of Rabbainu and his books.] This Reb Moshe traveled to Uman for Rosh HaShanah. When he was traveling back, it was Purim on the ship. He had a Megillah and they read it — and a Greek gentile passed by and spat on the Megillah. Reb Moshe raised his hand and gave him several proper slaps. The Greek went and complained to the captain — and the captain came with his officers and arrested Reb Moshe. They wanted to punish him and asked him truthfully: "Did you hit this Greek?" He answered yes. They asked why he hit him. He answered: "Because he disgraced and spat on the Ten Commandments." He then opened the Megillah to the passage of the Ten Sons of Haman, where the names are written in large letters, and showed them. He told them these were the Ten Commandments — and they counted the lines and said: "Yes, yes, you spoke truth — these are the Ten Commandments." And they thanked him for the slap and they themselves beat the Greek. [In truth: if he had shown them the Ten Commandments in the Torah scroll they would not have been as obvious, since the large letters in the Ten Sons of Haman are much more visible — and they believed him. And indeed it is written in the holy books that the Ten Sons of Haman correspond to the Ten Commandments.] Reb Moshe ultimately lived in Haifa, engaged in commerce, became wealthy, was generous and charitable — there is much to tell of his charity. And his name became renowned for praise throughout Haifa. And he brought close there a precious soul like himself — Reb Yehudah Rosenthal — whose righteousness, holiness, uprightness, and wholeness became renowned throughout Haifa. There is much to say about these two souls. And Reb Moshe ultimately lost his wealth through a wicked second wife, a relative of his, who robbed all his assets — and he also became indebted. And he wrote to me [asking that a disciple of Reb Yisroel of Kardan go to Reb Yisroel's grave in Tiberias to tell him of his troubles]. And this woman also suffered greatly — she contracted cancer and died from it. And the end was that Reb Moshe fell from his wealth entirely through her, and the house and property were taken for her debts. Out of mercy they rented him a small dark dwelling in a gentile's courtyard — with only one bed that he slept on, full of dirt and insects. And he became ill and weak throughout his body, his eyes dimmed from seeing, and all his limbs ceased to function. He had to go every day to the hospitality house to eat a piece of bread with a little tea — that was his sustenance. And so it was for some time. When we heard of this, trembling seized us and I could not believe it — and I traveled with the arousal of our fellowship and came to his dwelling. I literally could not understand how he could live there even one week, much less so many months. And I did not know him at all. I brought him to Jerusalem among our fellowship, and he was with us from the twenty-fifth of Elul until the twelfth of Nisan, when he passed away. Throughout all that time he never complained or said a word against Hashem — on the contrary, he always justified the Divine decree. When he was in Jerusalem he would tell me all the above and tell me he had been a disciple of Reb Nachman of Avrohovsky and served him — and that the primary arousal for his drawing close came through the letters of Reb Leibele Rubens, which were given to him to copy — and through this he was aroused and drew close to Rabbainu. And he told me he had heard from Reb Nachman that Rabbainu said: "I want to remain among you" — as cited in Chayay Moharan — there is in this an allusion that they should name their children Nachman: "Let each one have a Nachman in his house." "Yeder zol hobn a Nachmele." And he also told me that once Reb Nachman called him to him and said: "I have a request of you — promise me you will fulfill it." He promised. He said: "My request is that immediately after my passing, take the note that I am giving you now — on which I wrote 'bring him to Reb Nachman of Breslov' — and place it in his hand when you bury him, so that he will be buried with the note." And he said he was doing this so that if they ask where to bring him, he would show the note. And he fulfilled as he was commanded. And Reb Moshe had great vitality being among our fellowship, and had lodging near one of our fellowship who watched over him with food. And in the month of Nisan I traveled to Tzfas — and came back on the thirteenth of Nisan to Jerusalem. They told me of his passing — that they had found him in the morning, lying with his hands outstretched upward. And they accorded him the last honors and our fellowship even prayed in his room. And I was distressed that had I been present at his passing I would have done the note for him as he had done for his teacher. And one of our fellowship who had been watching over him with food told me that he had done this on his own initiative — even though he had not heard the story from him and knew nothing of it at all.

Reb Nachman of Tulchin went with Moharan'as on Ta'anis Esther in the late afternoon with the Megillah to pray Minchah. And Reb Nachman was already in high spirits [opgeboysmt] since Purim was close at hand. Moharan'as said to him: "Nachman — do you know why you are so cheerful? — You still have to say: 'For we are in great distress!'" "Nakhmen, veyst bist du azoy oyfgeboymt? — Fargest az du darfst nokh zogn 'Ki vetzarah gedolah anachnu'!" [This is said in the Anenu prayer of the Minchah Amidah on a public fast day — and Moharan'as reminded him that the fast is not yet over and proper seriousness is still required.]

The disciples of Rabbainu would give him written petitions requesting their needs — and they would also mention livelihood. But from the day they heard from Rabbainu the Torah of chapter 23: "You have commanded righteousness" — which teaches that the lust for money is [the source of great spiritual harm, and is connected to] "and I find bitterness more than death — the woman" — from then on they no longer requested livelihood. And so even today when people come to Rabbainu's holy grave, they request only spiritual matters and not physical matters. For when one comes to the holy grave, the physical is forgotten entirely — because one feels the lack of the spiritual far more intensely, and requests primarily the rectification of one's soul, and does teshuvah and repents of one's deeds, and asks to be worthy to serve Hashem properly. And in general all Breslov Chassidim — when they bless one another or ask one another to beseech Hashem on their behalf — request primarily only that they fulfill the will of Hashem and spiritual matters. And when they sometimes mention some physical matter, it is because it harms them greatly in spirituality and they cannot serve Hashem through it — therefore they mention it, so that it might be relieved and they could serve Hashem through it.

When people spoke to Moharan'as about a match after the death of his first wife, they told him about a woman who had several hundred rubles. He answered: "When there are several hundred rubles there are several hundred deaths — G-d preserve us. For when one has a hundred rubles there are a hundred deaths, G-d preserve us — and when one has two hundred rubles there are two hundred deaths, G-d forbid." [Meaning: when one does not use money in holiness — every hundred rubles of excess represents a spiritual death.]

The refined comportment that was with Rabbainu is impossible to estimate. And Rabbainu said: "Kings should send their sons to him to learn proper conduct." Once on the first night of Rosh HaShanah, Rabbainu was at the table with his people — and they grabbed the moitzi with honey [the challah for the honey]. Rabbainu became angry and said: "Like little children — the moitzi with honey!" "Azoy viya kleyne yunglikh — der moitzi mit honik!" And he went from the table and was not at the table with them that night because of this.

Rabbainu also said: "East is by his bundle" — meaning: when one prays Shemoneh Esrei on the road and determines where East is, Rabbainu said: "East is at his belongings so they should not be stolen." [Meaning: the main concern should be guarding one's things, not only the direction of prayer.] And when one of our fellowship suffered a loss or theft, Rabbainu would be angry at him and force him to travel and search for the lost item — even when the expenses for the search were greater than the value of the lost item. And so it was the practice of our fellowship, and Reb Avraham — when he lost even a handkerchief — would travel back until the handkerchief was found.

Reb Mordechai — Reb Dov Chiyalis — was accepted as rabbi in Teplik by command of Rabbainu, as cited in Yemei Moharan page 29, when Rabbainu was traveling to Uman. And Rabbainu said to the people of Teplik: "I am gifting you a pearl of a rabbi." "Ikh shenk aykh ferlekhen Rav." And when in the year 5571 he was in Uman for Rosh HaShanah, the great wealthy man of Uman, the wealthy man of Tulchin, made a wedding with a groom from the family of the commentators. Rabbainu told Reb Mordechai to go to the wedding. He went there, was honored, and sat next to the groom. They were given candy — and Reb Mordechai said which blessing should be made on the candy. The groom disputed with him that a different blessing should be made. And they debated with each other in Talmud, legal decisors, Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmud — for about three hours and more — until the groom forgot he was a groom and stood on one foot on the bench and his other foot on the ground. The groom's father — who was one of the legal commentators — was standing by the door outside listening to the debate. He entered and said to his son: "My son — this Jew is right in what he says." "Der Yid iz gerekhт." And afterward the groom said: "I did not believe that Chassidim can truly learn!" And once the great Gaon Reb Rivaley of Odes was a guest in Teplik, and there was a question there about a woman whose husband had disappeared — and Reb Mordechai stated his opinion and the other rabbi of Teplik stated his opinion. They brought in Reb Rivaley to rule on the matter — and he ruled like Reb Mordechai. And Reb Rivaley said: "In Teplik there are two rabbis — one is worth a thousand rubles and one is worth a patkel" [a coin of negligible value]. And once on motzei Shabbos Reb Mordechai was sleeping in his house in Teplik — and it was about midnight. There was a knock on his door. He asked: "Who is there?" The answer: "Shmuel Ayzik." He was greatly astonished — for Teplik was very far from Dashiv where Reb Shmuel Ayzik lived. He opened the door. Reb Shmuel Ayzik commanded him to take Havdalah and a cup of wine — and went with him to the cemetery. There Reb Shmuel Ayzik recited Havdalah — and Reb Mordechai heard one of the souls respond "Amen." And they returned home — Reb Mordechai to his house and Reb Shmuel Ayzik to Dashiv.

They told Moharan'as that the Magid of Dubna says in his rebuke: "There is not a single spark!" "Es iz nito kayn funk." Moharan'as answered: "There is a spark — but there is no one to blow it to fan the spark properly." "A funk iz do — nor es iz nito kayn blozer er zol tsi blozn dem funk." [Meaning: every Jewish heart yearns and burns for Hashem — only it is covered over with the dust of desires and sadness and worries — and what is lacking is a Tzaddik who can blow away the coarseness and awaken the spark in every heart to burn for Hashem.]

The holy Tzaddik of Berdichev said: "When the Days of Awe arrive, it stabs him in the back." "Az er kumt ימים נוראים shtekhт im di flide." And Moharan'as said about this: "One whom it does not stab — how much stabbing in the back he deserves!" "Der vos shtekhт im nit — vifl biz shoyн shtekhн!"

Reb Leib of Strestinitz was asked by the holy Tzaddik Reb Nachum of Chernobyl why he had no candelabra [i.e., no attached followers or wealthy supporters]. Reb Leib replied: "By me the candelabra are wandering and I sit in my place — and by you it is the opposite: you wander and the candelabra stand in their place." "Bay aykh zenen di lakhter in aykh iz noe vad — un bay mir bin ikh afn ort un di lakhter zenen noe vad." [Meaning: my followers wander and seek me out, while I remain fixed in my place of service. Whereas your situation is opposite.]

They told before Rabbainu about the holy Tzaddik Reb Shlomo Karliner who said: "If there are no fish on Shabbos — Shabbos is not Shabbos." "Azmen hot kayn fish nit af Shabes — iz der Shabes kayn Shabes nit." [For he was extremely strict about fish on Shabbos, and it is cited in Beis Aharon that he said: if there are no fish for Shabbos, one should worry more than what is written about worrying the entire year — meaning more than the worry of Yom Kippur.] Rabbainu answered: "What do fish have to do with Shabbos? Shabbos is Shabbos and fish is fish!" "Viya kumt Shabes tsi fish? Shabes iz Shabes un fish iz fish!" [Meaning: the strengthening of Rabbainu — that even if things are not as they should be, one must not fall from this. Shabbos exists and is holy regardless of fish.]

Rabbainu once saw a man walking with a tear in his garment in mourning for his deceased, G-d preserve us. Rabbainu said: "The sadness he had caused this death" — meaning: his habitual sadness had brought this bereavement upon him [as cited in Sefer HaMiddos — one must guard oneself from sadness so as not to come to bereavement, G-d preserve us].

Rabbainu said: "If Yom Kippur was not as it should be — at least let Shem Hashem [the day after Yom Kippur, which the world calls by a certain name] be as it should be." "Az der Yom Kipur iz nit geven viya es bадарfт tsi zayn — zol khatshe der gast nokh zayn viya es badarf tsi zayn." [Meaning: if Yom Kippur passed without proper devotion, one must strengthen oneself — for whenever one does good it is good. And so our fellowship say, in the name of Moharan'as: even if all of Shemoneh Esrei was not prayed properly — at least pray Elokai Netzor [the concluding prayer] properly — and so forth.]

They told before Moharan'as that the Tzaddik Reb Meir of Premishlan says about "Praise Him with timbrel and dance" [Hallel'uhu betof umachol]: he explains umachol as "and they will forgive" [u'yimcholu] — meaning: "Praise Hashem, for the end will be that they will forgive." "Lobt Hashem yisborakh — vorn der sof vet men moykhel zayn." Moharan'as replied: "So it is that they will forgive — but one won't escape the whip's blow." "Ader fun shmits vet men zikh nit aroys dreyen." [Meaning: yes, ultimately one will be forgiven — but the suffering that comes from sins cannot be avoided.]

Moharan'as said: "The holy Shelah — meaning the book Shelah HaKadosh — is Hashem's country estate [filvarkton], meaning it contains everything. And my Likutay Halachos is Hashem's Garden of Eden." And it is told: three did not have their books called by the name they chose — namely: the Rambam called his book Mishneh Torah [a great name] — yet the world calls it not by that name but only "Rambam." The Alshich called his book Toras Moshe [a great name] — yet the world calls it not by that name but only "Alshich." The holy Shelah called his book Shnei Luchos HaBris [a great name] — yet the world calls it not by that name but only "Shelah."

Reb Shimshon, grandson of Rabbainu — in his travels, sometimes he would hear how people weakened and spoke disparagingly of Rabbainu. He would pretend not to know who they were talking about and ask: "Who are you speaking of?" They would say: "The Breslover." He would ask: "Who is this Breslover?" They would reply: "Have you not heard of the Breslover? He is famous throughout the world!" He would say: "He is probably not of great lineage." They would reply: "On the contrary — he was of the greatest lineage that ever was — on both sides — a grandson of the Ba'al Shem Tov and a grandson of Reb Nachman of Horodenka — both sides traced back to King David, peace be upon him." He would say: "Then probably he was not a scholar." They would reply: "On the contrary — he was a scholar and a very great Gaon — for one sees his genius from his books." "Then probably he was not holy." "Heaven forbid — his holiness and asceticism are visible in his very books." "Did he make books?" "Certainly — and they illuminate the world." "And if so — why are you speaking of him?" "Because the Shpole Zeide spoke of him." "And where is this Shpole Zeide? Probably of great lineage?" "No — he is not a man of lineage — his father was a simple innkeeper." "Probably a great scholar?" "No — just a plain mind." "Probably holy and ascetic?" "Nothing known about his holiness." "He probably made great books?" "He made no books at all." And he replied: "Cursed of the cursed — may your ears hear what your mouths are saying! This one was of the greatest lineage on both sides — a scholar and very great Gaon — of great perception — very holy and ascetic — made books that illuminate the world. You speak of him — because someone spoke falsehoods about him: a simple innkeeper's son — of plain mind — nothing known of his holiness — no books at all. Is this conceivable?!" And they were left like mutes and could not answer a word.

Once the Elder of Shpola traveled to the holy Tzaddik of Berdichev to speak his folly — for this was his practice: to travel to Tzaddikim to slander Rabbainu and speak words of falsehood and fabricated testimony, to make them dispute Rabbainu. And at that time several other great Tzaddikim had gathered in the home of the holy Tzaddik of Berdichev — in order to excommunicate and ban the Elder for humiliating a genuine Torah scholar — namely Rabbainu — without cause, as cited in Chayay Moharan. But the wife of the holy Tzaddik of Berdichev disrupted the matter — she entered among them barefoot and confused the whole thing. And the Elder cursed her that her feet would develop [a certain affliction]. She was greatly afraid of the curse — and the disciples of the holy Tzaddik of Berdichev advised her to always wear black stockings so it would appear as if she had that affliction. And so she always walked in black stockings, as is well known. [The reason she gave herself to this so intensely on behalf of the Elder: the Elder supported her and gave her much money each year to distribute to the poor — and this bribed her. And Rabbainu said at that time that because of this, the punishment to the holy Tzaddik of Berdichev was that for an entire year he prayed with plain simplicity in the siddur like a child, and did not attain the perceptions he previously attained — for previously he would see the angels reciting song. And Rabbainu said they were taking all his levels from him — but Rabbainu had great mercy for all his toil and effort, for all his levels had come to him through great toil and effort. And in truth he was a faithful friend of Rabbainu. Once when Reb Levi Yitzchak was walking to the house of study, Rabbainu was then reciting the morning blessings. Reb Levi Yitzchak heard him and was very deeply moved and said: "Reb Nachmene's blessings ring throughout all the worlds." And Rabbainu himself would not allow any opposition to Reb Levi Yitzchak to penetrate — for he had mercy on him as described. And once Rabbainu saw through his holy spirit that the Elder was traveling to Reb Levi Yitzchak — and Rabbainu also traveled there, and they were together at his home, and peace was nearly made. But the Elder feared: what would the world say, and his own important followers — why had he disputed with Rabbainu for nothing? And once when Rabbainu saw that the Elder was going to Reb Levi Yitzchak, he sent Reb Noson and Reb Naftali, as cited in Yemei HaTela'os.]

And Rabbainu held the holy Tzaddik of Berdichev to be the greatest of the famous ones of his generation — and said of him that he is "prince over worlds." And of the holy Reb Baruch he said that he is "prince over myriads of myriads." And of Reb Levi Yitzchak he said his tallis-slippers were efficacious for rectification of the covenant. And of the Rav [the Seer of Lublin] he said he was "prince over a thousand" — but they are in Russia. And once the holy Tzaddik of Berdichev was at the home of the holy Reb Baruch, with other great Tzaddikim, and the Rav of Berdichev asked the question that had always been puzzling: since the Rambam and the Ra'avad constantly dispute — with the Ra'avad making objections on the Rambam — in what way are they equal? And all present were stumped. And he himself — the Rav of Berdichev — answered with great arousal and commotion — causing everything to fall from the table: "In this matter they are equal — in the Oneness of the Creator — in this they are completely equal!"

The holy Tzaddik Reb Shlomo Yitzchaki — who composed Rashi's commentary on the Torah and other works — had a wound in his throat. All the doctors despaired of healing him. The Rambam heard about this and Rashi traveled to him. When he came, the Rambam honored him and invited him to the midday meal. He prepared for him meat with almond milk — and hung the Rav [in his mind's eye] in the air and told him that this food was specifically meat with milk — and if he did not eat it he would kill him with a sword. And Rashi replied: then since this is mortal danger and there is no alternative, he would eat. And he ate. And from the greatness of the revulsion he felt at eating meat and milk — something forbidden by the Torah — he began to vomit — and from the vomiting the wound opened and he was healed. Afterward the Rambam told him that in truth it had been meat with almond milk, which is permitted — and asked him to forgive him for causing him distress, for he had seen that no other remedy would work except this — that through his great revulsion the wound would open. And a further story of a certain Gaon — Reb Yokil Hamburger who was a Chief Rabbi — is told as well [involving someone who struck him over a walking stick, mistaking him for a thief; and afterward came to apologize when he saw it was the Rav on the pulpit — and the Rav, thinking the man had returned to hit him again, kept pleading he had not taken the stick, until the truth became clear].
[This story has been incorporated into story 143-144 above, as both accounts concern the same subjects and appear consecutively in the source.]

The Rav Reb Shmuel Belin — author of Machatzis HaShekel on the Shulchan Aruch, and principally his commentary on the Magen Avraham. The world says he himself was the soul of the Magen Avraham — since the Magen Avraham is extremely concise and difficult to understand, he was compelled to return to this world to compose the Machatzis HaShekel to explain his own words. He was the rabbi in Kallin, and the Chasam Sofer was extremely submissive before him. When the Chasam Sofer's disciples would say "see what the world does," he would say: "See what Reb Shmuel of Kallin does — for he is the world." Reb Shmuel's custom was to give a plain Torah lesson before his congregation between Minchah and Ma'ariv. The Chasam Sofer very much wanted to hear his teaching — but could not, because the moment Reb Shmuel saw him he would not teach but would honor him. Therefore the Chasam Sofer hid himself under the bench and listened. Afterward, when the Chasam Sofer taught his own students and said one of those plain explanations, he would say: "Dos hob ikh geganvet bay Reb Shmuel." [This I stole from Reb Shmuel.] And the Gaon author of Ketzos HaChoshen — they tried to make him the rabbi in Frankfurt but they refused. His student, also a great Gaon, went to petition them to take his teacher as rabbi — and they refused, saying they did not know he could learn so well. When he printed his book Shev Shematesa they still dismissed him. But when he printed Ketzos HaChoshen on the Shulchan Aruch Choshen Mishpat — with extraordinary sharpness — and the copy reached the Gaon Reb Akiva Eiger, he took a horse and traveled specifically to the Gaon Reb Yaakov Alisa, author of Chavos Da'as, bringing the book with him, and showed it to him saying: "Look at what Hashem has in this world — a Jew like this who can learn so well!" "Zeyt vos der Aybershter farvakt af der velt — a Yid er zol kenen azoy gut lernen!"

Reb Avraham's disciples in Uman told me that Reb Avraham related to them [the elders of our fellowship] that the disciples of Moharan'as so cherished and loved Eretz Yisroel that when a letter came to them from Eretz Yisroel they would cherish even the postage stamp very much — that it had merited to be in Eretz Yisroel — and they would store it with their tallis and tefillin, saying: "Eretz Yisroel is tefillin and tefillin are also tefillin — so they should be kept together." And Reb Avraham himself — when he traveled for Rosh HaShanah, he would take with him a bottle of wine. And for every drink he drank in the Diaspora he would drip a drop from the wine he had brought from Eretz Yisroel into the cup — so that his drink would receive the holiness of Eretz Yisroel. And the bottle of wine was very precious to him and he was very sparing with it — only a single drop into each drink — so it would last through all the time he was in the Diaspora. Once Reb Avraham spoke with our fellowship about the holiness of Eretz Yisroel and said: "Do you think I am only saying that there are G-d-fearing people there and Eretz Yisroel helps them? There are also free-thinkers there — and Eretz Yisroel helps them too [that they are not as they were in the Diaspora]." And once one of our fellowship asked Reb Avraham whether he should travel to Eretz Yisroel. Reb Avraham certainly agreed [for he greatly encouraged our fellowship to travel to Eretz Yisroel and said every Jewish man should go to Eretz Yisroel]. And the man replied: "How can one travel away from the Rebbe?" Reb Avraham answered: "If it is your view that traveling to Eretz Yisroel means traveling away from the Rebbe — then you should indeed not go. But for me, when I travel to Eretz Yisroel I travel toward the Rebbe. [For the Tzaddik's primary place is in Eretz Yisroel — and Rabbainu said explicitly: 'My place is only in Eretz Yisroel — and for now I am pasturing in Breslov.'] And there is much more to tell of Reb Avraham on the matter of Eretz Yisroel." And Reb Avraham said that Eretz Yisroel is like a vessel of water placed on a fire — at first it seems clear, but when heated one sees it is full of sand. And the sand is poured off and it becomes clear again — until it becomes truly entirely clean. So it is with a Tzaddik and Eretz Yisroel: before coming to Eretz Yisroel it seems he is already a decent person — but when he comes, the truth is shown that he is not yet clean. And Eretz Yisroel gradually purifies him until he becomes truly clean.

And the story of Hershel of Ostropolia — who spoke jests as is known and would amuse the holy Reb Baruch — Rabbainu said of him: he was a Chassid who fell [meaning he had been a Chassid and could not hold himself from descending to jesting — which is an opening for the Other Side — and Rabbainu said a Chassid who has fallen is worse than a convert]. He came to Rabbainu, and Rabbainu hinted to his disciples that from whatever he said they should not answer him at all — to have no dealings with him. For he wanted specifically to bring Rabbainu and his disciples to laughter. But he could not do so in any manner — for no one answered him as described. And he left.

Once Moharan'as was asked what one sees in the Rav of Savran as evidence of his greatness. They replied: the arousal he has at the Kiddush of Friday night — with great passion and the movements he makes then, and so forth. Moharan'as replied: "This is not sincere" — "es iz nit ernsht" — for if it were truly genuine, such arousal would not always be in the same place and at the same time — only at the Kiddush and nowhere else. For how is it that he is always aroused precisely there and not in any other place? [For a person is always in motion and not always at the same level — sometimes the arousal comes in one place and sometimes in another. But not always only at the Kiddush and nowhere else.] And Rabbainu said of him and of Moharan'as that they were two fresh souls of the entire generation [meaning: as is written in the Ari's writings, almost all souls are reincarnations from previous generations, and only very few are truly new — and in that generation Rabbainu said that only those two were fresh souls. And the Rabbi of Savran could have merited greatly — but fame distracted him, for he was unwilling to relinquish fame].

[Several stories here in the source are recapitulations of accounts already recorded above in Parts 1 and 2, including the full Chanukah leap of Reb Nachum of Chernobyl and the fish/Shabbos exchange with Reb Shlomo Karliner. See stories 25 and 136 above for these full accounts.]

They told before Rabbainu about the holy Tzaddik of Volotishsk [who was Rabbainu's in-law] — that he said he had already been yearning and longing to ascend to Eretz Yisroel for forty years. And the holy Tzaddik of Khvilnik [also Rabbainu's in-law] said: "Why do they need to yearn so much? If they want to travel — just open the strongbox, take the money, and travel!" Rabbainu said: "This one will travel and arrive in Eretz Yisroel — and that one will not." For the primary thing is the will and the yearning.

And once Rabbainu said: "The primary obstacle that is harder and heavier than all else is only the obstacle of the mind [and the heart]. For if there is no obstacle of the mind — meaning: if there is no doubt in the mind, and one is absolutely determined that one must do this particular thing, and the will is strong — then whatever other obstacles there may be: his wife, all the people in the world opposing him, or money, or the sea — all would be broken by the strong will." [As the world says: "Will breaks iron."] Therefore if one does not complete a thing with one's will, this is a sign one did not truly want it — for there is nothing that stands against a true will. And in these words Rabbainu said: "The primary obstacle is the obstacle of the mind." [And once someone said to Rabbainu: "I want to be a decent person." Rabbainu replied: "Do you want to want more intensely?" — meaning: do you truly want with full force? For if there is a strong will, one certainly achieves what one wants. Only if one does not maintain the strong will — for the primary thing is the will, and nothing is stronger than the will.]
[This account has been recorded above in the composite entry for stories 147–155.]

Once they were speaking before Moharan'as about money and treasures. Moharan'as answered: "If one could obtain a treasure — I am swift and would run first to the treasure!" "Ikh bin a zariz — volt ikh gikher gekrigt dem oytser." [Meaning: everyone in the world chases and runs after "treasure" — worldly wealth — and this is all vanity and the evil inclination deceives the world. And meanwhile the world passes and no one truly obtains it. But Moharan'as said: I am swift — I have already found the true treasure — Rabbainu's path. As is already cited in Sefer HaMiddos: one who chases after hidden treasures shortens his days.]

The holy Tzaddik Reb Dov Ber, son of the holy Tzaddik Reb Shneur Zalman, the Rav of Liadi, said of Moharan'as that "he is an illui [a prodigy] in Chassidus." [Meaning: just as one says of a great Torah prodigy "he is an illui" — Reb Dov Ber applied this same description to Moharan'as in the realm of Chassidic avodah and service of Hashem.]

Reb Natan Leibele Rubens — a disciple of Moharan'as [from whose letters some are preserved] — was also among the young men who printed the book Likutay Tefilos. They toiled and exerted themselves greatly to purchase typeset letters to set the type — traveling abroad and purchasing type letters [against the government's wishes]. When Hashem helped and they brought the type letters to Moharan'as, he was full of joy — and then gave the sign for the printing of Likutay Tefilos: the initial letters spell out "Tachas ahavati yistenuни — va'ani tefillah" [In place of my love they accuse me — but I am prayer]. And Reb Natan Leibele Rubens was among the typesetters without any salary — and they did their work in Moharan'as's house without the knowledge of the government, for it was a great prohibition to print Rabbainu's books. And the opponents informed that there was a printing press in Moharan'as's house printing Rabbainu's books — and soldiers came out to search the house. And Reb Natan Leibele Rubens and his companions hid themselves under the beds while the soldiers searched the house. And Reb Natan Leibele Rubens danced under the bed in a whisper and said to his companion: "Now is doubly our beatitude!" [For what greater joy than being hidden under a bed for the sake of printing Rabbainu's holy books?] And when they finished Likutay Tefilos, they sealed the room of Moharan'as together with the books. Reb Nachman of Tulchin went up into the attic and broke through the roof — and descended and took the Likutay Tefilos books and hid them. And I saw one copy of Likutay Tefilos that had the censor's markings on the places that displeased the censor. And Moharan'as already wrote in his letters that there would be much to tell about what happened during the printing of Likutay Tefilos — and even when Mashiach comes they will speak much about it.

Blessed is Hashem forever, Amen and Amen. He has granted us to arrive this far. May it be His will that we merit all the remaining writings [of Rabbainu and Moharan'as] — to study from them and to live by them and to draw close to Hashem through them. Na Nach NaChMa NaChMaN MAyUMaN.
